raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), combining valsartan-mediated blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor with sacubitril-mediated augmentation of natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin and other vasoactive substrates. The concept emerged after omapatrilat, a vasopeptidase inhibitor, showed efficacy signals in heart failure but unacceptable angioedema related to simultaneous ACE and neprilysin inhibition [1,2]. By pairing neprilysin inhibition with an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than an ACE inhibitor, LCZ696 (sacubitril/valsartan) preserved neurohormonal counter-regulation while reducing angioedema risk. Early hypertension studies confirmed potent blood-pressure lowering and acceptable tolerability [3], and the phase 2 PARAMOUNT trial in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) showed greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) than valsartan, supporting dedicated outcome trials [4].

The pivotal evidence in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) comes from PARADIGM-HF, designed to test sacubitril/valsartan against evidence-based ACE inhibition with enalapril [5]. The trial was stopped early after showing a 20% relative reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, a 20% reduction in cardiovascular death, a 21% reduction in first heart-failure hospitalization and a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality [6]. Benefits extended beyond first events: sacubitril/valsartan slowed clinical progression, reduced urgent visits and treatment intensification, and improved symptoms and quality of life [7]. Mode-of-death analyses showed fewer sudden deaths and fewer deaths from pump failure, consistent with broad effects on ventricular biology and haemodynamics [8].

Subgroup analyses have been clinically important because sacubitril/valsartan is a chronic foundational therapy rather than a niche intervention. Efficacy was consistent across age groups, including older patients, although hypotension and renal vulnerability require careful titration [9]. Benefit persisted even when patients received doses below target, reinforcing continuation whenever tolerated [10]. Baseline systolic blood pressure modified tolerability more than efficacy; symptomatic hypotension was more frequent, but renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia and cough were generally less common than with enalapril [11]. In patients with diabetes, sacubitril/valsartan improved glycaemic control and reduced initiation of insulin or oral agents [12]. Renal analyses suggested slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate despite modestly increased albuminuria, implying complex intrarenal haemodynamic effects [13]. Among patients taking mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, severe hyperkalaemia occurred less often with sacubitril/valsartan than enalapril [14]. Patient-reported outcomes also favoured ARNI therapy, with less deterioration in physical and social activity limitations [15]. Interpretation of natriuretic peptides requires nuance: BNP may rise because it is a neprilysin substrate, whereas NT-proBNP remains the preferred biomarker for monitoring [16].

Implementation studies refined how to start therapy. TITRATION showed that both condensed and conservative up-titration strategies can achieve target dosing, with slower titration useful in lower blood pressure, lower prior renin–angiotensin system inhibitor dose or frailer patients [17]. PIONEER-HF moved ARNI use into the hospital, demonstrating that initiation after haemodynamic stabilization for acute decompensated HFrEF produced larger NT-proBNP reductions than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalaemia or angioedema [18]. Biomarker analyses showed parallel reductions in high-sensitivity troponin and soluble ST2, suggesting early effects on myocardial stress and injury [19]. TRANSITION confirmed feasibility of starting sacubitril/valsartan either before discharge or shortly after discharge [20], and PIONEER-HF extension data suggested that earlier initiation yields earlier clinical benefit [21].

Reverse remodelling provides a mechanistic bridge between biomarker change and outcomes. In PROVE-HF, NT-proBNP reduction after starting sacubitril/valsartan correlated with improvements in left ventricular volumes, ejection fraction and atrial volumes [22]. EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant short-term reduction in aortic characteristic impedance versus enalapril, but it supported safety and suggested favourable structural trends [23].

Evidence in HFpEF and mildly reduced ejection fraction is more graded. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for reducing total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death versus valsartan, but suggested greater benefit in patients with ejection fraction below the normal range and in women [24]. Pooled analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF indicate a continuous attenuation of benefit as ejection fraction rises, with the most compelling effect in HFrEF and heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction [25]. In advanced HFrEF, however, the LIFE trial did not show clear superiority and highlighted tolerability limitations, reminding clinicians that very low blood pressure, severe congestion and end-stage disease may constrain ARNI use [26].

Guidelines now position sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational HFrEF therapy, preferably replacing ACE inhibitors or ARBs in eligible patients, and as a consideration in selected patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, particularly at the lower end of the ejection-fraction spectrum [27,28]. Contemporary therapy increasingly combines ARNI with beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors; DAPA-HF suggested dapagliflozin benefits are consistent on background ARNI therapy [29]. Safety surveillance should focus on blood pressure, renal function, potassium, washout after ACE inhibitors, history of angioedema and affordability. Sex-specific PARAGON-HF analyses and broader pooled data underscore that “HFpEF” is biologically heterogeneous and that ARNI benefit is most plausible where congestion, natriuretic-peptide activation and subnormal systolic reserve coexist [30]. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan is among the most important therapeutic advances in HFrEF, with expanding but more selective roles across the wider heart-failure spectrum.
